newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African truth body quizzes Botha over apartheid.
newsitem.headline: S.African truth body quizzes Botha over apartheid.

text.p: South Africa's truth commission had sent former president P.W. Botha a written list of questions about murders and bombings against anti-apartheid activists, commission deputy chairman Alex Boraine said on Tuesday.
"The questions looked at his position as former minister of defence, prime minister and president and we hope that his answers will assist us in our work," Boraine said in a telephone interview.

"We do not want to speculate what he will do when he gets the questions, but we hope he will answer them... if he doesn't we will have to consider other options," Boraine said, adding that the list had been sent on Monday.
The commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, has the power to subpoena reluctant witnesses or suspected perpetrators of human rights abuses.
Botha, leader of the country during the turbulent 1980s, has been named by police officers as having given the orders for at least one bombing aimed at government opponents.

The leader of a security police hit squad, Eugene de Kock, who has been convicted of a series of murders, said during his trial last year that Botha and other senior politicians must have approved his squad's activities.

Tutu visited Botha last year to speak to him about the allegations. Botha said he had nothing to apologise for but added that he would be willing to consider answering written questions from the commission.

Botha is one of only two surviving presidents from the apartheid era. The other, F.W. de Klerk, has told the truth commission that Botha refused to cooperate in drafting a general submission on apartheid by the National Party.
De Klerk succeeded Botha as president and as leader of the party, which implemented apartheid after taking power in 1948 and began dismantling it in 1990.

President Nelson Mandela told a television interviewer in Davos, Switzerland, this week that the purpose of the truth commission was to uncover not the foot soldiers of apartheid but those who had given the orders.
The commission was set up last year to probe human rights violations during 30 years of South Africa's race conflict.
